title: Making AI Generative for Higher Education: Adoption and Challenges Among Instructors and Researchers
extended_summary:
This report examines how generative AI is being adopted in higher education teaching and research, with a focus on instructors’ and researchers’ experiences, challenges, and support needs. The central questions are how faculty, graduate students, and related academic personnel are using generative AI, how it is affecting teaching, learning, and research practices, what barriers they face, and what kinds of institutional guidance or resources they need. The paper is motivated by the rapid emergence of tools such as ChatGPT and the lack of clear consensus about effective, ethical, and sustainable uses in postsecondary settings.

The study is based on a collaborative qualitative research project involving 19 universities in the US and Canada. Institutional research teams, trained by Ithaka S+R, conducted semi-structured interviews between March and May 2024 using a shared interview guide. The total dataset included 246 interviews with people holding both teaching and research responsibilities, including faculty, postdoctoral scholars, and graduate students. A representative sample of 45 interviews was thematically coded using grounded-theory-informed qualitative analysis in NVivo. The report focuses on participants’ perceptions and self-described practices rather than testing a specific intervention or measuring causal effects.

In teaching and learning, the report finds that many instructors see AI integration as inevitable and are experimenting with ways to incorporate it, especially through AI-literacy-focused classroom activities. These activities often ask students to generate AI outputs and critically evaluate them, helping both students and instructors better understand the tools’ strengths and limitations. Instructors also reported using AI in their own workflows for preparing materials, generating assignments, and revising feedback. However, many remain uncertain about how AI aligns with course learning objectives, worry about over-reliance by students, and struggle with academic integrity policies. Participants commonly wanted more consistent institutional guidance while still preserving disciplinary flexibility.

In research contexts, adoption was also common but often exploratory rather than deeply integrated. Participants described using generative AI mainly for brainstorming, outlining, summarizing literature, and revising writing, but expressed caution about accuracy, ethics, and research integrity. Across both teaching and research, the paper concludes that higher education institutions need better discipline-specific support, clearer ethical guidance, improved AI literacy efforts, and secure, affordable access to vetted tools. Overall, the report portrays generative AI adoption as widespread but still unsettled, with experimentation outpacing the development of stable norms and best practices.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative AI chatbot/LLM used for text generation, brainstorming, summarization, drafting, and conversational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The report discusses ChatGPT as a commonly referenced generative AI tool in higher education, cited by interviewees using it for brainstorming, outlining, summarizing, revising writing, AI literacy activities, and exploring teaching/research workflows.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools broadly, including LLM-powered systems used for writing, summarization, brainstorming, coding assistance, feedback revision, and instructional support.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied through 246 qualitative interviews about how instructors and researchers in higher education are adopting generative AI in teaching, learning, and research; emphasis was on exploratory use, AI literacy activities, workflow support, academic integrity concerns, and support needs.

findings.finding_summary: Across 246 qualitative interviews, instructors reported widespread exploratory use of generative AI in teaching and learning, especially for AI literacy activities, assignment design, lecture preparation, and limited student coursework support. Perceived outcomes were mixed: some instructors said AI improved average work quality or reduced syntax-related barriers in coding, while others worried students were losing important underlying skills and that alignment with course learning objectives remained unresolved.
findings.measure: Qualitative interview themes on perceived teaching/learning effectiveness, alignment with learning objectives, and student skill development

findings.finding_summary: Interviewees described AI literacy-oriented classroom activities as highly successful for helping students critically evaluate generative AI outputs, including summaries, citations, and code. Instructors reported these activities improved students’ understanding of AI capabilities and limitations and also increased instructors’ own familiarity with the tools, though many described them as one-off experiments rather than established long-term practices.
findings.measure: Qualitative interview themes on AI literacy, critical evaluation skills, and understanding of tool limitations

findings.finding_summary: Instructors commonly reported that generative AI saved time in their own workflows by helping create activities and assignments, summarize information, prepare lectures, draft rubrics, and revise instructor-written feedback. However, they emphasized that outputs required substantial prompting, checking, and modification, so efficiency gains were mainly from producing a usable base structure rather than finished materials.
findings.measure: Qualitative interview themes on instructor workflow efficiency and time-saving in course preparation and feedback

findings.finding_summary: The interviews highlighted institutional challenges around generative AI governance: instructors wanted clearer top-down guidance on academic integrity, more coherent AI policies across courses, stronger discipline-specific support, and secure, affordable tool access. At the same time, many valued institutional flexibility and instructor autonomy, creating tension between standardization and disciplinary variation.
findings.measure: Qualitative interview themes on policy coherence, governance, support needs, and institutional implementation

findings.finding_summary: In research contexts, over half of interviewees had tried generative AI for brainstorming, outlining, revising writing, summarizing scholarship, and literature support, but use was usually minimal and experimental. Respondents were optimistic about efficiency and acceleration potential, yet concerns about accuracy, ethics, and maintaining research quality and integrity limited sustained adoption.
findings.measure: Qualitative interview themes on research workflow support, experimentation, and barriers to sustained use

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical qualitative interview study with 246 participants, providing useful directional evidence about adoption, perceptions, and reported uses, but it does not provide experimental or quasi-experimental causal estimates of effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: Impacts are reported as perceived and mixed, with no quantified effect sizes or standardized outcome measures. The paper suggests promising efficiency and AI literacy benefits but also unresolved concerns about learning trade-offs and institutional implementation.
